title: Water at the festival, and a city divided
sum: Jesus' brothers urge him to show himself at the Festival of Shelters in Jerusalem. He refuses, then goes up quietly, and halfway through the festival he begins teaching in the temple courts. The whole chapter is a running argument in public: Is he a good man or a deceiver? Where did he learn? Is he the Messiah, or the Prophet, or neither? Can the Messiah come from Galilee? The crowd splits, the authorities send guards to arrest him, and the guards come back empty-handed, overwhelmed by how he speaks.

On the last great day of the festival, when priests poured water from Siloam on the altar and prayed for rain, Jesus cries out: "If anyone is thirsty, he should come to me and drink." John explains that he meant the Spirit, to be given after Jesus is glorified. The chapter ends with the rulers scorning the crowd that "does not know the law," and with Nicodemus, one of their own, asking for a fair hearing.
readings: Read as a trial

John tells chapters 7–8 as a trial held in the temple courts. Witnesses speak for and against Jesus, the authorities try to arrest him, the law is cited on both sides (7:19–24, 51), and the crowd acts as a divided jury. The reader is asked to give the verdict that the characters cannot agree on.
Read through the festival

Every major saying in chapters 7–8 picks up a part of the Festival of Shelters: living in shelters recalls God's care in the wilderness, the water rite recalls the rock that gave water and prays for rain and for the river of Ezekiel 47, and the giant lamps recall the pillar of fire. Jesus presents himself as what the festival celebrates.
Read for John's own readers

Late in the first century, John's readers argued with Jewish neighbors about the same questions: where Jesus came from, whether he kept the law, whether any leader had believed in him (7:48). The chapter gave them answers, and also showed people in the story who believed and were afraid to say so (7:13).

views.H: The detail fits Jerusalem before AD 70 closely: the festival's water rite, the temple police under the chief priests, Solomon's Porch, debates known from later Jewish texts about the Messiah's origin and about circumcision overriding the Sabbath. John's outline, with several visits to Jerusalem for festivals, is often judged more realistic than the single visit in Mark.
views.C: Many critical scholars see signs of editing: 7:15–24 continues the argument of chapter 5, so some think chapters 5 and 6 have been swapped, or that the Gospel was written in stages. The debates reflect the time of writing as well as Jesus' time: who has "believed" among the rulers (7:48) was a live question for the Johannine community.
views.L: John uses misunderstanding and irony throughout: the crowd thinks it knows where Jesus is from (7:27), the leaders mock that he will go to the Greeks (7:35), and the rulers curse the crowd for not knowing the law while breaking it themselves (7:49–51). The reader knows more than every character.
views.J: The chapter shows a lively Jewish debate, with many opinions among Jews: some call Jesus good, some a deceiver, some the Prophet, some the Messiah. "The Jews" in 7:1, 11 and 13 must be the authorities, since everyone in the scene is Jewish. Jewish scholars note that the arguments Jesus uses, such as reasoning from circumcision to healing, are recognizably rabbinic.
views.T: The Orthodox Church reads 7:37–52 with 8:12 as the Gospel at Pentecost, passing over the story of the adulterous woman. Augustine read the living water as the Holy Spirit poured into believers (Tractates on John 32). The words "the Spirit was not yet" were used in later debates about when and how the Spirit is given to the church.

deep.h: The Festival of Shelters in Jesus' day
deep.b:
Shelters (Sukkot) was the last great pilgrim festival of the year, after the harvest of grapes and olives. The law asked Israel to live in shelters made of branches for seven days, to rejoice before the LORD, and to keep an eighth day of closing assembly (Leviticus 23:33–43; Deuteronomy 16:13–15). Josephus calls it the holiest and greatest Jewish festival.

Two rites described in the Mishnah (tractate Sukkah 4–5) are especially important for John 7–9:

  • The water-drawing. Each morning a priest filled a golden pitcher at the pool of Siloam and carried it up to the altar with trumpets sounding, where it was poured out beside the wine offering. The rite asked God for the winter rains, and was tied to prophecies of water flowing from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8; Ezekiel 47:1–12). Jesus' cry in 7:37–38 belongs here.
  • The lights. In the Court of Women four huge lampstands were lit, and men danced through the night with torches. Jesus' "I am the light of the world" (8:12) is spoken "in the treasury area" (8:20), in that same court.

The healing in chapter 9 brings both together: Jesus, the light of the world (9:5), sends a man to the waters of Siloam, and he comes back seeing. Zechariah 14 also pictured the nations coming up to keep the Festival of Shelters, a hope that stands behind 7:35 and 10:16.

deep.h: Who did people think the Messiah would be?
deep.b:
Chapter 7 is the New Testament's best window on popular debates about the Messiah. The crowd raises several expectations:

  • His origin will be hidden (7:27), a view also found in Justin's Trypho, in 1 Enoch and in 4 Ezra.
  • He will come from David's family and Bethlehem (7:42), from 2 Samuel 7 and Micah 5.
  • He will do signs (7:31), though the Old Testament does not clearly say the Messiah would work miracles.
  • The Prophet like Moses (7:40) may be a different figure from the Messiah, as in the Dead Sea Scrolls.

John lets every expectation be voiced and none be simply confirmed. His answer is that Jesus' origin is with the Father, "from above," which no expectation fully covered.

echoes: Leviticus 23:33–43; Deuteronomy 16:13–15; Deuteronomy 18:15–19; Zechariah 14:8; Zechariah 14:16–19; Ezekiel 47:1–12; Isaiah 12:3; Isaiah 55:1; Exodus 17:6; Psalm 78:16; 2 Samuel 7:12; Micah 5:2; 2 Kings 14:25; Mark 6:1–6; Mark 3:21; Revelation 22:1–2

settings.when: shortly before the Festival of Shelters, in autumn, about six months before the last Passover
settings.why: The brothers press him to prove himself in Jerusalem, the way a public figure would. Jesus refuses to let family or crowds set his timing: his "moment" belongs to the Father. Knowing that the speakers are his own unbelieving family sharpens the point: even those closest to him misread him.
settings.readers: For John's readers, many of whom faced family pressure or rejection, the scene showed that Jesus too was misunderstood at home, and that his brother James's later faith (1 Corinthians 15:7) came after Easter.

settings.what: Teaching in the temple: where his teaching comes from
settings.to: "the Jews" in the temple courts, here the teachers and authorities, and the crowd of pilgrims
settings.when: about the fourth day of the Festival of Shelters
settings.why: Answering the question of his learning, Jesus says his teaching comes from the one who sent him, and then defends his Sabbath healing at Bethesda (chapter 5) by an argument his hearers used themselves: if circumcision may be done on the Sabbath, so may making a whole person well. The goal is to move them from judging by appearances to judging rightly.
settings.readers: John's readers were accused of following an unlearned teacher who broke the Sabbath. The speech gave them his answer in the terms of Jewish law.

settings.to: Jerusalemites in the temple, who knew the authorities wanted him dead
settings.why: The Jerusalemites wonder whether the authorities' silence means they believe. Jesus cries out that they know his hometown but not the one who sent him. His words aim to unsettle their certainty about origins and point to the Father.
settings.readers: For later readers the passage answers the objection, "We know Jesus came from Nazareth, so he cannot be the Messiah."

settings.to: the crowd and the temple guards sent to arrest him
settings.when: during the festival, as the arrest is ordered
settings.why: Faced with guards, Jesus speaks calmly of his departure to the Father, which no arrest can prevent. The hearers misunderstand and joke that he will go to the Greeks.
settings.readers: John's readers, some living among Greeks in the Dispersion, saw the joke come true in their own churches.

settings.to: the crowds of pilgrims in the temple courts
settings.when: on the last, great day of the festival, during or after the water-drawing rite
settings.why: At the moment the people were praying for water and remembering water from the rock, Jesus offers himself as the source of living water. The purpose is invitation: come and drink. John's comment says the promise looks ahead to the Spirit.
settings.readers: For John's readers, who had received the Spirit after Jesus' glorification, the passage explained their own experience and linked it to Israel's festival.

settings.by: the chief priests and Pharisees, the guards, and Nicodemus
settings.to: one another, in a closed meeting of the authorities
settings.when: the same day, after the guards return without Jesus
settings.why: The leaders try to explain away the guards' failure and the people's interest: no ruler has believed, and the crowd is ignorant. Nicodemus reminds them that the law requires a hearing. The scene shows the opposition hardening against its own rules.
settings.readers: John's readers knew of leaders who believed in secret (12:42) and of hostility from synagogue leaders; Nicodemus stood for the first group.

settings.what: The woman caught in adultery (a later addition)
settings.by: the scribes and Pharisees, and Jesus
settings.to: Jesus, in the temple courts, with the people looking on; then Jesus to the woman
settings.when: early one morning in the temple; the story's original setting in Jesus' life is unknown, since it was added here later
settings.why: The question is about the Torah's law (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22–24), which ordered death for both adulterers on the evidence of witnesses. The accusers want to trap Jesus between Moses and Rome, which, John 18:31 says, did not allow Jewish courts to execute (historians debate how strictly that held). Jesus does not set aside the law but asks whether the accusers are fit to carry it out, and then sends the woman away uncondemned with a command to stop sinning.
settings.readers: The story circulated on its own in the early church, and was used in the 200s in Syria to urge bishops to receive repentant sinners (the Didascalia). It was placed in John later, perhaps because of 8:15, "I am not judging anyone."
views: Most scholars, conservative and critical, think it is an early tradition about Jesus, preserved outside the four Gospels and added to John later.
A minority, mostly defenders of the Byzantine text, argue it was in John from the start and was removed because it seemed too lenient on adultery, as Augustine reported.
Mary remained a virgin always. The "brothers" were close relatives, such as cousins; James and Joses of Mark 6:3 are sons of another Mary (Mark 15:40). This follows Jerome's answer to Helvidius.

Mary is "ever-virgin." The brothers were sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage, an old tradition found in the second-century Protevangelium of James and defended by Epiphanius; the Orthodox liturgy honors James as "the Brother of the Lord."
Luther and the Lutheran confessions called Mary "ever virgin" and so did not take the brothers as her sons; many Lutherans today leave the question open or read them as Mary's younger children.

Calvin, on Matthew 1:25, called Helvidius ignorant for concluding that Mary had other sons, and Zwingli also taught that she remained a virgin. Many Reformed Christians today read the brothers as Mary's sons.
John Wesley believed Mary "continued a pure and unspotted virgin" after Jesus' birth (Letter to a Roman Catholic, 1749). Methodists today generally leave the question open.

The brothers were younger children of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus, as the plain reading of Matthew 1:25 and Mark 6:3 suggests. This was the view of Helvidius in the 300s; it is held by most Baptists and many other Protestants today, though not by the early Reformers.

title: The light of the world, and before Abraham
sum: The chapter opens with the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11), which the oldest manuscripts do not have; it was added to John later, though it may preserve a true memory of Jesus. Accusers bring her to trap him between Moses and Rome; he writes in the dirt, invites the sinless to throw the first stone, and sends her away uncondemned: "Go, and from now on, do not keep on sinning."

Then the Festival of Shelters debate goes on. Beside the great lamps in the temple, Jesus says, "I am the light of the world." The argument grows sharper with every exchange: about testimony, about his Father, about his going away, about freedom and slavery, and about who are Abraham's true children. It reaches its hardest words in 8:44, "You come from your father, the devil," and its highest claim in 8:58, "Before Abraham came to be, I am." His hearers pick up stones, and Jesus leaves the temple.
readings: Read as a family quarrel

Every speaker in this chapter is Jewish, arguing over Israel's Scriptures, Abraham and the Father. Read as a quarrel inside a family, the harsh words on both sides ("Samaritan," "demon," "devil") sound like the bitter language of a split that was happening in John's day between Jews who followed Jesus and those who did not.
Read as revelation

Read as John's theology, the chapter climbs through Jesus' identity: the light of the world (8:12), the one from above (8:23), the "I am" that must be believed (8:24, 28), the Son who frees slaves (8:36), and the one who existed before Abraham (8:58). Each answer provokes a deeper question until the claim is made in God's own words.
Read after the Holocaust

Since the twentieth century many Christian and Jewish readers have read this chapter with the history of its misuse in view. They ask how to keep its claims about Jesus while refusing its use as a verdict on the Jewish people, and how to translate "the Jews" honestly without spreading contempt.

views.H: The setting is precise: the treasury in the Court of Women (8:20), where the great lamps of the festival stood. The questions raised, about witnesses, Abraham's children and the Samaritans, are real first-century Jewish questions. Historians are divided on how much of the long speech goes back to Jesus himself.
views.C: Most critical scholars hear the voice of the Johannine community in chapter 8: the "Jews who had believed" (8:31) may be Jewish Christians who would not accept the community's high claims about Jesus, and the polemic of 8:44 reflects a painful separation late in the first century. The story of the adulteress is universally recognized as a later addition to John.
views.L: The chapter is built as a rising sequence of "I am" sayings, from "I am the light of the world" (8:12) to the bare "I am" (8:24, 28, 58). John's irony runs through it: the accusers guess he will kill himself (8:22), and in a sense he will give up his life; they ask if he is greater than Abraham, and the reader knows the answer.
views.J: Jewish scholars such as Adele Reinhartz point out that 8:44 has done real harm and argue that it cannot simply be explained away; others, such as Amy-Jill Levine, urge Christians to read it as an intra-Jewish argument and to stop using it against Jews. Traditions about Abraham seeing the future (Genesis Rabbah, 4 Ezra, Jubilees) help explain 8:56.
views.T: The church read 8:58 as one of the clearest claims to Christ's eternal divinity. Athanasius and the Nicene party cited it against Arius, and the Catechism of the Catholic Church links it to the divine name of Exodus 3:14. Augustine's sermon on the adulteress, "Two were left: misery and mercy," shaped Western preaching on forgiveness.

deep.h: A later addition: the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11)
deep.b:
The evidence. The story is missing from Papyrus 66 (about 200) and Papyrus 75 (about 175–225), from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (300s), and from most early manuscripts from Egypt, Syria and the East; two pages now lost from Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Ephraemi were too short to have held it. No Greek church writer comments on it before Euthymius Zigabenus in the 1100s, and Origen, Chrysostom and Cyril of Alexandria pass straight from 7:52 to 8:12 in their commentaries. The first Greek manuscript to contain it is Codex Bezae (400s). Where it does appear, many manuscripts mark it with signs of doubt, and it wanders: after John 7:36, 7:44 or 21:25, or after Luke 21:38 (family 13). Its language is more like Luke's than John's.

The story is old. Eusebius reports that Papias (about 120) told of a woman accused of many sins before the Lord, a story also in the Gospel according to the Hebrews (Church History 3.39.17). The Didascalia, a Syrian church order of the 200s, tells a version to urge bishops to receive repentant sinners. In the West, Ambrose, Jerome and Augustine knew it; Jerome included it in the Vulgate and said it was found in many Greek and Latin copies (Against the Pelagians 2.17); Augustine thought some had removed it out of fear that it excused adultery.

What scholars conclude. Almost all agree it was not part of John as first written. Many believe it is a true story from early tradition that the church refused to lose. Editions print it in different ways: NA28 puts it in double brackets; SBLGNT and THGNT leave it out of the text and give it in their apparatus; most English Bibles print it in place with a note, as here. See the variant on 7:53 and the card below.

deep.h: "Your father the devil" (8:44): who heard it, and what was done with it
deep.b:
In the story. Jesus is speaking in the temple to fellow Jews who, John says, had believed him (8:31) and who then defend their descent from Abraham and want to kill him (8:37, 40, 59). The sentence is part of an argument about whose children they are, judged by what they do: Abraham's children would do Abraham's works; those who seek to kill show the family likeness of the first killer. It is not a statement about Jewish birth or race; Jesus has just said, "I know you are Abraham's seed" (8:37).

In its world. Fierce family language was common in Jewish disputes. The Dead Sea Scrolls call other Jews "sons of darkness" and men of Belial; the prophets called Israel's leaders rebels and "offspring of an adulteress" (Isaiah 57:3); John the Baptist called a crowd "brood of vipers" (Matthew 3:7). The same Johannine writings say of Christians who hate their brothers that they are "children of the devil" (1 John 3:10).

What was done with it. Once Christians were a separate and then powerful religion, they read 8:44 as a description of the Jews as a people. It fed the medieval picture of Jews as allies of Satan, appears in Luther's On the Jews and Their Lies (1543), and was quoted in Nazi propaganda: Elvira Bauer's 1936 children's book Trust No Fox opens with the line "The father of the Jews is the devil." After the Holocaust, the Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate (1965) declared that Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, and many Protestant and Orthodox bodies have made similar statements. Scholars still disagree about how far the Gospel itself is to blame: Adele Reinhartz argues that its rhetoric is anti-Jewish in its effect whatever the author meant, while others stress that it is an inner-Jewish quarrel misread by later Gentile Christians. Either way, using this verse against Jews today misreads it.

Chapter 8 contains three of the Gospel's absolute "I am" sayings, with no picture after them: "unless you believe that I am" (8:24), "then you will know that I am" (8:28), and "before Abraham came to be, I am" (8:58). In the Greek Old Testament, God speaks this way in Isaiah 43:10, where the people are to believe hoti egō eimi, "that I am," and God's name in Exodus 3:14 begins egō eimi in the Greek. The progression ends in a claim of existence before Abraham and the response of stoning, the penalty for blasphemy. Most readers, ancient and modern, conclude that John presents Jesus as sharing the identity of Israel's God. Others read "I am he" as a messianic claim only, and Jehovah's Witnesses translate 8:58 "I have been," a claim of existence before Abraham as a created being. See the topic page and the card below.

echoes: Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 17:6–7; Deuteronomy 19:15; Deuteronomy 22:22–24; Exodus 3:14; Exodus 13:21; Isaiah 43:10–13; Isaiah 42:6; Psalm 27:1; Numbers 21:8–9; Genesis 3:4; Genesis 4:8; Genesis 15:6; Genesis 17:17; Genesis 21:10; Genesis 22:8; Luke 21:37–38; Galatians 4:21–31; 1 John 3:8–12

settings.what: "I am the light of the world"
settings.to: the Pharisees and others in the Court of Women, by the treasury
settings.when: at the Festival of Shelters, beside the great lamps lit during the festival
settings.why: Jesus claims to be what the lamps of the festival pointed to, God's light leading his people. When the Pharisees object that a man cannot be his own witness, he answers with the law's rule of two witnesses: himself and the Father. The aim is to bring them to follow the light, not to win a legal point.
settings.readers: For John's readers, Jesus' testimony stood even when his human witnesses were rejected.

settings.what: "Where I am going, you cannot come"
settings.to: "the Jews" in the temple, the same audience
settings.when: continuing the dispute at the festival
settings.why: Jesus warns that unless they believe "that I am," they will die in their sins, and that when they lift up the Son of Man they will know who he is. The words are a warning meant to lead to faith, and John says many did believe (8:30).
settings.readers: John's readers knew that the "lifting up" meant the cross, and read the warning in that light.

settings.to: "the Jews who had put their trust in him" (8:31), who then argue with him; probably the wider crowd as the argument grows
settings.when: continuing the dispute at the festival
settings.why: Jesus tells new believers that true discipleship means staying in his word and being freed from sin. When they claim freedom as Abraham's descendants, he argues that children show their father by their deeds, and that their wish to kill him reveals another father. The words are meant to break their confidence in descent and to call them to the Son who frees.
settings.readers: Most scholars think John's readers heard this through their own conflict with Jewish neighbors and with Jewish believers who did not share their view of Jesus. Later Christians wrongly made it a verdict on all Jews; see the chapter page.
views: The audience are people whose belief was real but shallow; Jesus' demand exposes it.
The scene reflects later Jewish Christians whom the Johannine community regarded as having fallen away.
The new believers of 8:31 are not the same as those who argue from 8:33 on.

settings.what: "Before Abraham came to be, I am"
settings.to: "the Jews" in the temple, his opponents in the debate
settings.when: at the end of the long dispute at the Festival of Shelters
settings.why: Accused of having a demon, Jesus answers that whoever keeps his word will never see death, that Abraham rejoiced to see his day, and finally that he existed before Abraham. The hearers take it as blasphemy and reach for stones. The purpose is to make the final claim plain, so that the hearers must decide.
settings.readers: For John's readers, this was the clearest answer to the question "Who are you?" (8:25), and the ground of their worship of Jesus.

traditions.q: Is the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11) Scripture?
views: Yes. The Council of Trent received the biblical books "with all their parts" as they were read in the Church and contained in the Latin Vulgate, which includes this story; Catholic scholars such as Raymond Brown accepted it as canonical Scripture while judging that it was not written by John.

It is part of the Greek text the Orthodox Church received, and the Patriarchal edition of 1904 prints it in place. It is not read at Pentecost, when the reading passes from 7:52 to 8:12, but in the Byzantine lectionary John 8:3–11 is read on the feasts of penitent women saints, such as St Pelagia (8 October). Its place in the Church's worship, not its date of writing, settles its authority.

Calvin accepted it, saying it had long been received in the Latin churches and was found in many old Greek manuscripts, and contained nothing unworthy of an apostle. Reformed churches hold that the Scriptures in their original Hebrew and Greek are the final authority, so many Reformed scholars now treat it as a true story that was not part of John.

Divided. Many evangelical scholars, such as D. A. Carson, conclude it was not part of John and should be read as early tradition rather than preached as Scripture; others, including defenders of the King James Version and the Byzantine text, hold it is fully Scripture.

traditions.q: Does Jesus' "before Abraham came to be, I am" (8:58) claim to be God?
views: Yes. In saying "I AM" Jesus takes to himself the divine name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14), and his hearers understood it as a claim to divinity; the Son is eternal, "begotten, not made."

Yes. The fathers, especially Athanasius against the Arians, read 8:58 as the Son's eternal existence with the Father; the icon of Christ bears the letters ho ōn, "the One who is," from the Greek of Exodus 3:14.

Yes, as Protestant churches in general hold. Calvin read 8:58 as Christ claiming an eternity that belongs to God alone, and the Westminster Confession calls the Son "very and eternal God, of one substance and equal with the Father" (8.2).

No. The New World Translation renders "before Abraham came into existence, I have been": Jesus existed in heaven before Abraham as God's first creation, but the phrase is not the divine name, which belongs to Jehovah alone.

Yes, in their own sense: Jesus Christ was Jehovah, the God of the Old Testament, before his birth, so he can speak as the I AM. Latter-day Saints understand the Father and the Son as two distinct divine beings, not one substance.

title: The man born blind sees, and the seeing go blind
sum: Jesus sees a man blind from birth. His disciples ask whose sin caused it; Jesus says no one's, and that God's works will be shown in him. He spreads clay made with spit on the man's eyes and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam, and the man comes back seeing. It is a Sabbath.

The rest of the chapter is an investigation. Neighbors argue whether it is the same man; the Pharisees question him twice and his frightened parents once, because anyone who confessed Jesus as Messiah would be put out of the synagogue. The man, who has nothing to lose, grows bolder with every answer, until he lectures his judges and is driven out. Jesus finds him, and the man believes and worships. The chapter ends with a reversal: the blind man sees, and those who are sure they see are judged blind.
readings: Read as a sign

The healing is the sixth sign in John and enacts Jesus' saying "I am the light of the world" (8:12; 9:5). The man's physical sight leads to spiritual sight, and the story is a picture of coming to faith: slowly, under pressure, against authority.
Read as a two-level drama

Since J. Louis Martyn, many scholars read the chapter as telling two stories at once: Jesus healing a man in Jerusalem, and believers in John's day being questioned and expelled from synagogues for confessing Jesus. The man's courage was a model for them. Critics of this reading caution that we have little evidence for such expulsions at that date.
Read as baptism

Early Christians called baptism "enlightenment," and this chapter was read to people preparing for baptism in Lent: washing in water named "Sent," receiving sight, confessing "I believe, Lord," and worshiping. Catacomb paintings show the scene.

views.H: The pool of Siloam, rediscovered in 2004, was a large stepped pool at the south end of the city. Sabbath rules about kneading and healing are known from Jewish sources, and saliva was a common ancient remedy. Many historians accept that Jesus was remembered as healing the blind (Mark 8:22–26; 10:46–52).
views.C: The chapter is the main evidence for Martyn's theory that John's community was expelled from the synagogue around the time of the Birkat ha-Minim. Critics such as Kimelman, Boyarin and Reinhartz argue the evidence for a formal ban is late, and some think 9:22 projects later conflict onto Jesus' lifetime.
views.L: One of the most carefully built scenes in the Gospels: seven scenes, two characters on stage at a time, a beggar who grows into a witness, and judges who shrink into the accused. Irony is everywhere: "We know" say the leaders, and know nothing; "I don't know," says the man, and sees.
views.J: Jewish readers note that the Pharisees are divided (9:16) and argue from the Torah, as careful judges should, and that the expulsion of 9:22 is unlikely to reflect Jesus' own day. The chapter has been used to portray Jews as willfully blind; Jewish and Christian scholars today warn against reading "the Jews" here as a people.
views.T: In Latin and Eastern churches the chapter was read in Lent as preparation for baptism, called "illumination" by the Greek fathers. Irenaeus saw in the clay a new act of the Creator who formed Adam. Eastern Orthodox churches read it on the Sunday of the Blind Man, after Easter.

deep.b:
The disciples' question assumes what many in the ancient world assumed: that disability is a punishment. Jesus denies it outright: neither the man nor his parents sinned (9:3). That denial has mattered greatly to disabled readers and to anyone who has been told that suffering is proof of guilt (compare Luke 13:1–5; Job).

His next words raise a new problem: the man was born blind "so that God's works can be shown" in him. Some read this as God's plan using a long affliction for a good end; others, troubled by a God who would cause blindness for a display, punctuate the Greek differently so that the purpose belongs to Jesus' work, not to the blindness (see the note at 9:3). Either way the chapter refuses to treat the man as a lesson: he speaks for himself, argues well, and is the hero of the story.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the chapter acts out both rites of the festival
deep.b: This is my own reading, though it overlaps with commentators who link chapter 9 to the Festival of Shelters (for example Raymond Brown). At the festival, two rites stood out: water drawn from Siloam and poured out on the altar, and great lamps lit in the temple. In 7:37–38 Jesus claimed the first ("come to me and drink"), and in 8:12 the second ("I am the light of the world"). In chapter 9 he joins them in one act: as "the world's light" (9:5) he sends a man to the very pool the water came from, and the man receives light. John even translates Siloam as "Sent" to point at Jesus, the one sent. If this is right, the healing is not a new episode after the festival but its climax, and the festival's prayers for water and light are answered in a beggar outside the temple.

echoes: Exodus 4:11; Exodus 20:5; Ezekiel 18:20; Genesis 2:7; Joshua 7:19; Isaiah 6:9–10; Isaiah 29:18; Isaiah 35:5; Isaiah 42:7; Psalm 66:18; Psalm 146:8; 2 Kings 20:20; Mark 8:22–26; Mark 10:46–52; Luke 13:1–5

settings.to: the disciples, as they pass the man in Jerusalem
settings.when: after the dispute at the festival, possibly still during it
settings.why: The disciples treat the man as a theological puzzle. Jesus redirects them from blame to work: the night is coming, and while he is in the world he is its light. The words are meant to change how the disciples see suffering people.
settings.readers: John's readers lived after the "night" of Jesus' departure and were the "we" who must now do the works (9:4).

settings.what: The investigation of the healed man
settings.by: the Pharisees, called "the Jews" in 9:18–22, the man and his parents
settings.to: the healed man and his parents, questioned by Pharisees acting as a court
settings.when: soon after the healing, on or after the Sabbath
settings.why: The authorities must decide whether a Sabbath healing can be from God. The question was real: a sign that broke the Sabbath might be a test like the one in Deuteronomy 13. The man's answers press them toward the conclusion they refuse. Knowing they are judges explains the oath formula "Give God the glory" and the expulsion.
settings.readers: For John's readers, many of whom had been or feared being put out of the synagogue, the man was their model: an ordinary person who would not deny what Jesus had done.
views: The scene mirrors expulsions of Jewish Christians in John's day (Martyn, Brown).
The parents' fear reflects local pressure in Jesus' lifetime, described in later words (Carson, Keener).

settings.what: "Do you believe in the Son of Man?"
settings.to: the healed man, after he was driven out; then Pharisees standing nearby
settings.when: the same day, after the expulsion
settings.why: Jesus seeks out the man the community rejected and brings him to faith. To the Pharisees who overhear, he speaks of judgment: those who admit blindness can be given sight, but those who insist they see remain in their sin.
settings.readers: John's readers learned that when they were put out, Jesus came to find them.

title: The good shepherd and the Festival of Dedication
sum: Jesus goes on speaking to the Pharisees who claimed to see. He tells a word picture of a sheepfold: thieves climb in over the wall, but the shepherd comes through the door, calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. Then he explains it: he is the door, the way to safety and pasture, and he is the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep and has other sheep to gather into one flock. No one takes his life from him; he lays it down and takes it back. His hearers split again.

Months later, at the Festival of Dedication (Hanukkah) in winter, the Jews surround him in Solomon's Porch and demand a plain answer: is he the Messiah? He says his works testify, that his sheep hear his voice and no one can snatch them from his hand or the Father's, and: "I and the Father are one." They take up stones for blasphemy. He answers from Psalm 82, "You are gods," and slips away to the place beyond the Jordan where John had baptized, where many believe in him.
readings: Read through Ezekiel 34

The chapter is a commentary on Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's shepherds who feed themselves, promises to shepherd his sheep himself, and promises one shepherd, David. Jesus claims to be both God's shepherding and the promised David.
Read through Hanukkah

Hanukkah celebrated the temple made holy again after a pagan king defiled it, and the courage of leaders who gave their lives for Israel. Jesus speaks at that festival of himself as the one the Father "made holy" and as the shepherd who gives his life, contrasting himself with bandits and false deliverers.
Read as a word to church leaders

Pastors (Latin for "shepherds") have long read the chapter as a mirror: the hired man who runs, the thief who takes, and the good shepherd who knows each sheep by name and gives his life. 1 Peter 5:2–4 and Acts 20:28–29 apply the picture to elders.

views.H: Sheepfolds, doorkeepers and hired shepherds fit village life in Judea. Solomon's Porch on the east of the temple and the winter setting of Hanukkah are accurate details. The Festival of Dedication was a young festival, about two hundred years old, celebrating the Maccabees' victory.
views.C: Critics note that 10:1–18 continues chapter 9 without a break and that 10:19–21 refers back to the healing, while 10:22 begins a new scene months later; some scholars think the order has been rearranged or that sayings from different settings were joined. The "other sheep" (10:16) are often read as Gentile believers in John's community.
views.L: John blends images freely: Jesus is both the door and the shepherd, and the sheep, the hired man, the thief and the wolf each stand for something without the picture becoming a strict allegory. The theme of voice ties the chapter together: the sheep know the shepherd's voice (10:4, 27), and those who are not his sheep do not.
views.J: Shepherd imagery for God and for Israel's leaders is deeply Jewish (Psalm 23; Psalm 80; Ezekiel 34). Hanukkah is the only Jewish festival from after the Old Testament that the New Testament mentions. Jewish readers note that the stoning attempts show a serious charge of blasphemy, and that Jesus answers with a Jewish argument from a psalm.
views.T: The good shepherd was one of the earliest Christian images, painted in the Roman catacombs. Councils and fathers cited "I and the Father are one" against both Arius and Sabellius. The Catholic Church calls the Fourth Sunday of Easter "Good Shepherd Sunday" and reads John 10 then, and Christians of many traditions have built teaching on the security of believers on 10:28–29.

deep.b: In the ancient Near East kings were called shepherds of their people; Hammurabi calls himself one in the prologue to his laws. Israel applied the title to God (Psalm 23:1; Psalm 80:1; Isaiah 40:11), to Moses and to David, who was taken "from following the sheep" (Psalm 78:70–72). When leaders failed, the prophets attacked them as shepherds who scattered the flock (Jeremiah 23:1–4; Zechariah 11). Ezekiel 34 is the closest background to John 10: shepherds who feed themselves, sheep scattered and devoured by wild animals, God's promise "I myself will search for my sheep," and then "I will set over them one shepherd, my servant David" (Ezekiel 34:11, 23). Jesus speaks to leaders who have just thrown a sheep out (9:34) and claims the role God promised to take for himself.

Hanukkah ("Dedication") remembers the events of 167–164 BC, when the Seleucid king Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the temple and Judas Maccabeus led a revolt, cleansed the temple and rededicated the altar (1 Maccabees 4:36–59). In Jesus' day it was an eight-day festival of joy and lights in December, remembering God's deliverance and Israel's resistance to pagan rule. Its themes run through 10:22–39: consecration ("the one the Father made holy," 10:36), true and false leaders who deliver or destroy the flock, and blasphemy, since Antiochus was remembered as a king who made himself a god (Daniel 11:36). The question "Are you the Messiah?" fits a festival that celebrated a past deliverer. The later story of the oil that lasted eight days is found first in the Babylonian Talmud (Shabbat 21b), not in Maccabees or Josephus.

echoes: Ezekiel 34:1–31; Ezekiel 37:24; Psalm 23:1–4; Psalm 80:1; Psalm 82:6; Psalm 118:20; Numbers 27:16–17; Jeremiah 23:1–6; Zechariah 11:4–17; Isaiah 40:11; Isaiah 56:8; Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Maccabees 4:36–59; Hebrews 13:20; 1 Peter 2:25; 1 Peter 5:2–4

settings.to: the Pharisees who said "We see" (9:40–41), with the disciples and others listening
settings.when: right after the healing of the blind man, in Jerusalem, around the Festival of Shelters
settings.why: Spoken to leaders who had just thrown a healed man out, the word picture contrasts thieves and hired men with the true shepherd who knows, leads and dies for the sheep. It warns the leaders and claims for Jesus the role Ezekiel 34 promised. Read without its audience, it sounds like a gentle pastoral picture; with its audience, it is a sharp judgment on failed leadership.
settings.readers: John's readers, cast out like the blind man, heard that they belonged to a flock with a shepherd, and that "other sheep" from outside Israel were being gathered in.
views: The "other sheep" are Gentile believers (most interpreters).
They are scattered Jewish or separated Christian groups in John's day.

settings.what: At the Festival of Dedication: "Are you the Messiah?"
settings.by: "the Jews" in the temple, and Jesus
settings.to: "the Jews" who surround him in Solomon's Porch, probably including the temple authorities
settings.when: at Hanukkah, in winter, about two months after the Festival of Shelters
settings.why: They demand a plain answer about messiahship at a festival that celebrated a deliverer. Jesus points to his works, says his sheep hear his voice and are kept safe, and claims unity with the Father. When they move to stone him for blasphemy, he argues from Psalm 82 that Scripture itself calls those who received God's word "gods," so his claim cannot be dismissed out of hand. The aim is to move them to believe the works, if not the words (10:38).
settings.readers: John's readers were defending their worship of Jesus as the Son who is one with the Father; the passage gave them both the claim and an argument from Scripture.

traditions.q: Can those Jesus holds in his hand ever be lost (10:28–29)?
views: No. Those whom God has chosen and called can neither totally nor finally fall away from grace, but will persevere to the end, because God keeps them (Westminster Confession 17; Canons of Dort, fifth head).

No. Those who are truly saved will never fall away; they are kept by God's power. Some Baptists stress that true believers will persevere in faith, others that salvation once received cannot be lost (Baptist Faith and Message, article 5).

No one can snatch the sheep from Christ's hand, but the sheep can stop following; a believer who turns away from faith can fall from grace (Wesley, Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints).

Believers are kept by God through Word and Sacrament, but they can lose faith and the Holy Spirit by deliberate sin and unbelief; the Augsburg Confession rejects the view that the justified cannot lose the Holy Spirit (article 12).

God's grace is enough to keep believers, but grace can be lost through mortal sin and restored through repentance and the sacrament of reconciliation; final perseverance is a gift no one can be certain of without special revelation (Council of Trent, session 6).

Salvation is a lifelong growth into union with God, in which human freedom works together with God's grace. No outside power can snatch believers from God, but a believer can turn away through sin and unbelief, so final salvation is hoped for, not assumed.

traditions.q: Who are Jesus' "sheep," and why do some not believe (10:26)?
views: The sheep are those the Father gave to the Son before they believed; they believe because they are his sheep, and others do not because they are not (10:26, 29; 6:37, 44). Calvin read the verse so.

People become sheep by hearing and following; those who are not sheep are so by their own refusal, which Jesus still invites them to give up (10:38). God's grace goes before every person and enables a free response.

God's grace is the cause of faith, and God wills all to be saved; the Church teaches both predestination to glory and real human freedom, and Catholic theologians have long disagreed about how they fit together.

Those who believe owe their faith wholly to God's grace, but those who are lost are lost by their own fault, not by God's choice; Lutherans reject a predestination to damnation (Formula of Concord, article 11).
Gentiles called into the one Church with believing Israel under one shepherd, Christ; the verse is also read as a call to the unity of all Christians.
The elect among the Gentiles, gathered by the preaching of the gospel into one people with the believing remnant of Israel.
Gentile believers who, together with Jewish believers, form the church, a new body distinct from Israel as a nation, whose own promises remain for the future.

The descendants of Israel in the Americas: in the Book of Mormon the risen Jesus tells the Nephites, "you are they of whom I said: Other sheep I have" (3 Nephi 15:21), and says there are still others among the lost tribes.
Faithful worshipers who hope to live forever on a paradise earth, distinct from the "little flock" of 144,000 who will rule with Christ in heaven (Luke 12:32; Revelation 7:4, 9).
